clue.text: Pig scabs for fashionable bar snack

indicators.note: read as 'able to be fashioned', the letters before it are there to be shaped into something new

parts.note: eleven letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A trendy bar serving pork scratchings, the crispy bits of pig skin, as its snack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fashionable' looks like it praises the snack, but it is the anagram signal, read as 'able to be fashioned'. In Britain crisps are what Americans call potato chips.
explanation.definitionFit: A packet of potato chips is the standard thing ordered with a drink in a British pub.

clue.text: Beckoned eastwards, Lukashenko approved Russia's 'Union State' primarily, here?

definitions.text: Beckoned eastwards, Lukashenko approved Russia's 'Union State' primarily, here?

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so each word contributes only its opening letter

parts.words: Beckoned eastwards, Lukashenko approved Russia's 'Union State'
parts.note: the initial letters of the seven words

explanation.surface: Pulled toward the east, a strongman leader signs up to a political union with Moscow.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the wordplay and a description of the place. Lukashenko is the long-time president of this country, and the Union State is its treaty arrangement with Russia.
explanation.definitionFit: The clue describes the eastern European country ruled by Lukashenko that joined Russia in the so-called Union State.

clue.text: Norse god's surrounded — Odin's head — finally, finally wanting boats

indicators.note: wanting means lacking, so the word it governs loses its last letter
to surround something is to enclose it, so one piece goes around another

parts.note: taken as written
N is a dictionary abbreviation for Norse

indicators.note: the head of a word is its front, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: the first letter of the Norse chief god's name
finally means at LAST, and the second 'finally' says that word's final letter goes

explanation.surface: A Viking god, under siege, at last does without his longships.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's of 'god's' stands for 'has': the god has surrounded N. Then 'finally' is both a word meaning LAST and, repeated, an instruction to lose that word's final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Gondolas are the long flat-bottomed rowing craft of Venice, so they are a kind of boat.

clue.text: Ravenously eat up course

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading from the bottom, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: to wolf food is to eat it greedily

explanation.surface: Greedily wolfing down a course of a meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Course' looks like a dish at dinner, but it is the definition, meaning the way water runs.
explanation.definitionFit: A river's course is its movement along a path, the same idea as its steady stream or current.

clue.text: Pay attention: ready money's invested. Upset? Mostly upset

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the word drops its final letter
cash that is invested is put into a business, so one piece is placed inside another

parts.note: taken as written; 'ready money' also hints at the readies, British slang for cash
M is a standard abbreviation for money

indicators.note: upset in a down entry means turned upside down, so the letters run the other way

parts.note: upset as in knocked over is SPILT, and most of it loses the T

explanation.surface: A money adviser urges you to listen: your cash has been invested, and you are upset about it.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'Upset' is the fodder word, meaning spilt; the second 'upset' turns most of it upside down.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom is an emphatic command to listen closely and take seriously what the speaker is about to say.

clue.text: Musical instrument, one that squeals, is taken up

indicators.note: in a down entry, taken up means lifted from the bottom, so the letters read backwards

parts.note: a rat is an informer, one who squeals to the police
taken as written

explanation.surface: An instrument that squeals is picked up by a player.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One that squeals' suggests a noisy instrument, but it is slang for an informer.
explanation.definitionFit: The sitar is a long-necked plucked stringed instrument from India.

clue.text: Not half easy navigating two-master that's slight

indicators.note: not half means one half is dropped, so only part of the word stays
a vessel navigating moves through water, so this piece sits within the other letters

parts.note: the second half of the word
a ketch is a sailing boat with two masts

explanation.surface: Sailing a two-masted yacht is far from easy if the vessel is a flimsy one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not half' is British slang for 'very', so the surface says the sailing is very easy; in the wordplay it means half the word goes.
explanation.definitionFit: Something sketchy is thin and lacking detail, as is a slight piece of work.

clue.text: Fresh evasion, audacity: that's rich at the table!

parts.note: hot as in just made, hot off the press
to fudge is to dodge an issue
sauce is cheek or impudence

explanation.surface: Someone protests at a cheeky dodge in an argument over dinner: 'That's rich!'
explanation.walkthrough: 'That's rich' is an exclamation at someone's nerve; at the table it literally describes a rich dessert topping.
explanation.definitionFit: This thick sweet chocolate topping poured over ice cream is famously rich, and it is served at the table.

clue.text: They'd collared criminal without pity

indicators.note: something criminal is crooked or bent, so the letters are twisted out of order

parts.note: thirteen letters taken as written

explanation.surface: The police arrested a crook and showed him no mercy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Criminal' looks like the person the police caught, but it is the signal to rearrange the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting cold-heartedly means behaving without warmth or compassion, so with no mercy or sympathy at all.

clue.text: Disney World's setting for V. Woolf novel

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the Florida city that is home to the theme park resort
second meaning: Virginia Woolf's 1928 novel about a gender-changing poet

explanation.surface: A theme park becomes the backdrop for a literary novel.
explanation.walkthrough: V. Woolf is Virginia Woolf, the English modernist novelist; her book and the Florida city share a name.
explanation.definitionFit: The Florida city hosts the Disney resort, and the same name is the title of Woolf's fantasy biography.

clue.text: '20s style red coat altered

indicators.note: altered means changed, so the letters take a different order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A red coat restyled in the fashion of the 1920s.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue looks like dressmaking; the coat's letters are the raw material.
explanation.definitionFit: Art Deco is the geometric design movement that flourished in architecture and decoration during the 1920s and 1930s.

clue.text: Very much game for movie set in N. Dakota

parts.note: as in far better, very much better
Go is the Japanese board game

explanation.surface: Someone is very keen to see a film set in North Dakota.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Very much game' reads as 'really up for it'; split, it is two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: The Coen brothers' 1996 crime film takes its title from a city in North Dakota where part of it is set.

clue.text: The writer pulled back, tensed up, given a cuddle

indicators.note: pulled back means drawn in the opposite direction, so the letters run the other way

parts.note: the setter refers to himself
bracing oneself means tightening up in readiness

explanation.surface: An awkward author recoils and stiffens when someone hugs him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The writer' is the usual crossword way for the setter to say 'me'.
explanation.definitionFit: To be embraced is to be held in someone's arms, which is exactly a hug or cuddle.

clue.text: What may get you arms half akimbo, sweaty and gasping at the end?

definitions.text: What may get you arms half akimbo, sweaty and gasping at the end?

indicators.note: what may get you a thing is what produces it, so the gathered letters are rearranged to form it

parts.note: the first half of the word
taken as written

indicators.note: half means only part is kept, here the front two of four letters

parts.note: the last letter

indicators.note: at the end points to the final letter of each word it follows

parts.note: the last letter

explanation.surface: An exercise class that leaves you contorted, sweating and out of breath by the finish.
explanation.walkthrough: A composite anagram: the letters gathered from four places are rearranged, and the whole clue also describes the activity.
explanation.definitionFit: This form of yoga is done in a heated room, so the poses leave practitioners twisted, sweating and breathless.

clue.text: In the altogether bald lie, he's preposterous

definitions.note: the definition is a phrase meaning undressed; the answer is the state, as in 'in deshabille'

indicators.note: preposterous means absurd or nonsensical, so the letters fall into a senseless new order

parts.note: ten letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A naked man tells a barefaced lie, and an absurd one at that.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the altogether' is British slang for naked, from 'in the altogether nude'.
explanation.definitionFit: Deshabille, from French, is a state of being partly or carelessly dressed, close to having no clothes on.

clue.text: Discussed obscure monster of literature

indicators.note: something discussed is spoken about, so the word is given by its sound

parts.note: to obscure something is to conceal it

explanation.surface: Critics talk about a shadowy villain from a classic book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Obscure' looks like an adjective for a little-known monster, but it is a verb meaning conceal.
explanation.definitionFit: Mr Hyde is the murderous alter ego of Dr Jekyll in Stevenson's novella, a monstrous figure of fiction.

clue.text: Without walls round US prison, spy finally escaping

indicators.note: the final letter escaping means it gets away, so the word loses its end

parts.note: O is round in shape
pen, short for penitentiary, is American slang for a prison
a spy planted inside an organisation is a PLANT, minus its last letter

explanation.surface: A spy breaks out of an American jail that seems to have no walls around it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without walls' looks like part of the jailbreak story but is the definition. A plant is a mole or undercover agent.
explanation.definitionFit: An open-plan office or home has few or no internal partitions dividing its space into separate rooms.

clue.text: Language in Poetry: volume missing

indicators.note: missing means absent, so that letter is taken out

parts.note: verse is another word for poetry
V is the usual abbreviation for volume

explanation.surface: A book with a missing volume, apparently titled 'Language in Poetry'.
explanation.walkthrough: The italics make it look like a book title, which is why 'volume' seems natural.
explanation.definitionFit: Erse is an old name for the Gaelic language of Scotland or Ireland, a crossword favourite.

clue.text: Do foes struggle to secure end of Nicola Sturgeon, perhaps?

indicators.note: to secure is to hold fast, so one piece holds another inside it
a struggle is a disordered tussle, so the letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: six letters taken as written

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, the only one kept

parts.note: the final letter

explanation.surface: Political opponents fight to bring down Nicola Sturgeon, the former Scottish First Minister.
explanation.walkthrough: Sturgeon here is the fish, not the politician; 'perhaps' flags it as one example of the category.
explanation.definitionFit: The sturgeon is a large fish eaten for its flesh and roe, making it one example of edible marine produce.

clue.text: French dish: mash pear evenly, for thin crinkled sheets

parts.note: the crêpe is a French pancake
pap is soft mushy food

indicators.note: evenly points to the even-numbered positions, so only the second and fourth letters stay

parts.note: the second and fourth letters

explanation.surface: A recipe step: make a French dish by mashing a pear smoothly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mash' looks like an anagram signal for the fruit, but it is a noun meaning PAP, soft food.
explanation.definitionFit: Crepe paper is thin tissue with a crinkled texture, sold in sheets for decorations and crafts.

clue.text: Run for seconds of baked goods in celebrations

indicators.note: one thing for another means swapped in its place, so one letter replaces another

parts.note: pasties are pastry parcels with a savoury filling, like the Cornish pasty
R is the cricket abbreviation for run
S is the abbreviation for second

explanation.surface: Someone at a party goes back for second helpings of the pastries.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seconds' looks like extra helpings, but it is S, the time abbreviation, which is swapped out of the pastry word.
explanation.definitionFit: Parties are social gatherings held to mark an occasion, so they are a kind of festivity.

clue.text: Like Eric Clapton, narcoleptic?

parts.note: surface reading: the rock guitarist is said to fall asleep without warning
setter's reading: the two items share exactly the same eleven letters, so each is a rearrangement of the other

explanation.walkthrough: The comma makes it read as gossip about the guitarist's health; the real link is the letters, and the question mark warns that the definition is playful.
explanation.definitionFit: Words formed by rearranging the same letters are what this term describes, and the guitarist's name and the medical adjective are a perfect pair.

clue.text: Heading off, intellectual given to falls?

indicators.note: with the heading taken off, the word loses its first letter

parts.note: a clever, bookish person is brainy

explanation.surface: A clumsy academic leaves and keeps tripping over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Falls' suggests tumbling, but it means rainfall; the question mark flags the playful definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Weather that is prone to downpours is wet, and rain is what falls from clouds.

clue.text: Angel or shark?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a hospital carer, often called an angel for their kindness
second meaning: a sluggish, bottom-dwelling species of shark that shares the carer's name

explanation.walkthrough: Angel and shark look like opposites, saint against predator, which hides that one word covers both.
explanation.definitionFit: Hospital carers are affectionately called angels, and the nurse shark is a real species of shark.

clue.text: A little unpicturesque person of old

indicators.note: a little of something is only a small portion, so the letters are a short stretch inside a longer word

parts.note: letters three to six of the word

explanation.surface: Someone from the past who was not much to look at.
explanation.walkthrough: The Picts were an ancient people of what is now Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: The Picts lived in northern Britain in late Roman and early medieval times, so each was a person of long ago.

clue.text: Children regularly rejected your pizza (old sausage)

parts.note: CH is the dictionary abbreviation for child or children

indicators.note: regularly rejected means every other letter is thrown out, keeping the ones between

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters
O is the abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: The kids refused your pizza, which was topped with stale sausage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rejected' looks like the children turning down the pizza, but with 'regularly' it tells you to discard alternate letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Chorizo is a spicy Spanish pork sausage flavoured with paprika, often used as a pizza topping.

clue.text: Around wife, Everyman shall repeatedly feud

indicators.note: around means on both sides, so two pieces enclose the middle one

parts.note: the setter is 'I', and I shall contracts to I'll
W is the abbreviation for wife
the same contraction again

explanation.surface: The setter admits he will keep quarrelling with his wife.
explanation.walkthrough: Everyman is the setter, so 'Everyman shall' is 'I shall'.
explanation.definitionFit: A feud is lasting hostility between parties, and ill will is the animosity underlying such a quarrel.

clue.text: With alcohol banned by trains, I'm mixing cocktails

parts.note: a dry place or event has prohibited alcohol

indicators.note: mixing means stirring together, so the letters are jumbled into a new order

parts.note: eight letters taken as written

explanation.surface: Alcohol is banned on the trains, but a barman is mixing drinks anyway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mixing cocktails' reads as one phrase about bartending, but the first word signals the anagram and the second is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A dry martini is a classic mixed drink of gin with a little vermouth, so the plural names several such drinks.
